parts.article:
The plan to bring an asteroid to Earth
 
Moving in orbit around our Sun are millions of rocks known as asteroids. Now scientists have plans to capture one.
 
(A) Send a robot into space, catch an asteroid and bring it back to Earth’s orbit. This, say scientists and engineers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), could be feasible. A four-day workshop was dedicated to investigating the feasibility of capturing a near-Earth asteroid, bringing it closer to our planet and using it as a base for future manned space-flight missions. This is not something the scientists are imagining could be done someday in the future. It is possible with the technology we have today and could be accomplished within a decade. A robotic probe could anchor to an asteroid with simple magnets or grab it with specialised claws. Alternatively, a large spacecraft could use its gravitational field to shift the orbit of a larger asteroid, sending it towards Earth. ‘Once you get over the initial reaction — You want to do what?! — it actually starts to seem like a reasonable idea,’ says engineer John Brophy, who helped organise the workshop. In fact, many of these ideas have been on the drawing board for years as part of NASA’s planetary-defence programme against large space-based objects that might threaten Earth. And there’s no shortage of potential targets: NASA estimates there are 19 500 asteroids at least 100 metres wide within 45 million kilometres of Earth.
 
(B) Though rearranging the heavens may seem an excessive undertaking, this US mission has its merits. The US already has plans to send astronauts to a near-Earth asteroid, a mission that would mean confining them in a tiny capsule for three to six months and would involve all the risks of a deep-space voyage. Instead, robots could bring an asteroid close enough for them to get there in just a month. An asteroid would provide a stationary base from which to launch missions further into space. There are several advantages to this. For one, launching missions carrying materials from Earth requires a lot of power, fuel and, consequently, money, because of our planet’s strong force of gravity. Since this would be far weaker on an asteroid, materials mined there could be more easily taken off the asteroid and shuttled around the solar system. Many asteroids have a lot to offer. Some are rich in metals, which can be mined and used to build space-based habitats, or brought back to Earth. Others are up to one-quarter water, which could be used for life-support or broken down into hydrogen and oxygen to make fuel. Astronomers would also have the chance to get a close-up look at one of the solar system’s earliest relics, generating important scientific data. ‘Executing the asteroid-retrieval plan would help demonstrate and greatly expand mankind’s space-based engineering capabilities,’ says engineer Louis Friedman, another co-organiser of the Caltech workshop. For instance, the mission would teach engineers how to capture an unco-operative target, which could be useful practice for planetary-defence missions in the event of a threat from a meteoroid or comet approaching our planet,’ he adds.
 
(C) Former astronaut Rusty Schweickart, co-founder of the B612 Foundation, an organisation dedicated to protecting Earth from asteroid strikes, points out that although it would be technically feasible, shifting such a hefty and substantial target would not be easy: ‘You’re moving the largest mother-lode imaginable,’ he says. Engineers would need to be absolutely certain they could control such a potentially dangerous object. ‘It’s the opposite of planetary defence; if you do something wrong you have a Tunguska event,’ says engineer Marco Tantardini from the Planetary Society, referring to the powerful 1908 explosion above a remote Russian region thought to have been caused by a meteoroid or comet.
 
(D) Still, these obstacles only add to the appeal of the project for engineers, who love to go over every potential difficulty in order to solve it. And if the challenges posed by a large asteroid seem too daunting, researchers could always start with a smaller asteroid, perhaps two to ten metres across. Last year, Brophy helped conduct a study to look at the feasibility of bringing a two-metre, 1 000-kilogram asteroid — of which there might conceivably be millions — to the International Space Station. The study suggested the asteroid could be captured robotically in something as simple as a large bag. Of course, such a small object might not have the same emotional impact as a larger target. ‘NASA isn’t going to want to go to something that is smaller than our spaceships,’ says engineer Dan Mazanek from NASA’s Langley Research Center.
 
(E) No matter the size of the asteroid, these plans would require hefty investments. Even capturing a small asteroid would consume at least a billion dollars. Convincing taxpayers to foot such a bill could be difficult. However, private industry might be interested in getting involved. One possibility would be to push the asteroid into near-Earth orbit and then invite anyone who wants to develop the capabilities to reach and mine the object. However, although the undertaking might be scientifically exciting and provide great insight into the solar system’s formation, this is not enough on its own to justify the expense of bringing an asteroid to Earth. Investigations of asteroids can be done much more cheaply with an unmanned spacecraft, says chemist Joseph A. Nuth from NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. According to Brophy, ultimately we would be working towards bringing an asteroid closer to Earth in order to help humanity move out into the solar system.

reference:
Q14

干扰 不要被最后一句提到的“NASA防御计划”误导选 iii，那只是背景提及，段落核心在于论证“现在就能做”。

句子 (Section A) "This is not something the scientists are imagining could be done someday in the future. It is possible with the technology we have today..."

解析 A段反复强调该计划“可行（feasible）”、“不是幻想（not imagining）”、“现在就有技术（possible with the technology we have today）”，对应选项 v（一个可实现的目标，而非不可能的梦想）。

Q15

解析 B段详细列举了该任务在实际操作（作为基地）、经济（开采金属和水）、科研（数据）和防御演练等多方面的理由，对应选项 viii。

干扰 虽然提到了“metals”和“water”，但不要只看细节，全段都在讲“merits（优点/理由）”，涵盖了实用、经济和研究三个维度。

句子 (Section B) "Though rearranging the heavens may seem an excessive undertaking, this US mission has its merits... provide a stationary base... rich in metals... generating important scientific data."

Q16

解析 C段强调移动如此巨大的目标（hefty target）不容易，一旦出错会引发“通古斯大爆炸（Tunguska event）”般的灾难，因此暗示需要极高的技能和小心，对应选项 i。

干扰 看到“protection”或“defence”不要误选 iii，这一段是在强调操作的难度和风险，而不是介绍“最安全的保护方法”。

句子 (Section C) "Engineers would need to be absolutely certain they could control such a potentially dangerous object. ‘...if you do something wrong you have a Tunguska event’..."

Q17

干扰 看到“emotional impact”不要走神，核心在于“start with a smaller asteroid”这个策略调整。

解析 D段提出如果大行星太难，可以先从“smaller asteroid（更小的小行星）”开始，甚至用袋子就能装下，即从简单的入手，对应选项 vii（从一个较不具挑战性的任务开始）。

句子 (Section D) "And if the challenges posed by a large asteroid seem too daunting, researchers could always start with a smaller asteroid..."

Q18

解析 E段讨论了巨大的“投资（investments）”需求，提到“说服纳税人（convincing taxpayers）”很难，可能需要“私营企业（private industry）”参与，全段都在讲如何获得支持/资金，对应选项 iv。

干扰 这一段虽然有不同人的观点，但核心围绕着“bill（账单）”、“expense（开销）”和“justify（正当理由）”，即争取项目的支持。

句子 (Section E) "Convincing taxpayers to foot such a bill could be difficult. However, private industry might be interested in getting involved."

Q19

解析 B段末尾 Friedman 认为该任务能教工程师如何捕捉目标，这对未来的“行星防御任务（planetary-defence missions）”是有用的练习，对应选项 E（获得的技能可让地球免于未来危险）。

干扰 “Planetary-defence” 就是 “save Earth from danger”，逻辑完全对应。

句子 (Section B) "...which could be useful practice for planetary-defence missions in the event of a threat from a meteoroid or comet..."

Q20

句子 (Section C) "...shifting such a hefty and substantial target would not be easy: ‘You’re moving the largest mother-lode imaginable,’ he says."

干扰 “Hefty” 和 “largest mother-lode” 都在强调 “weight/size”，导致了 “not be easy” (challenging)。

解析 C段开头 Schweickart 指出，虽然技术可行，但移动如此“hefty（沉重/巨大）”的目标绝非易事，对应选项 D（小行星的重量使项目极具挑战性）。

Q21

解析 D段末尾 Mazanek 说 NASA 不会想去一个“比我们要去的飞船还小（smaller than our spaceships）”的地方，即对太小的目标没兴趣，对应选项 B。

干扰 “NASA isn't going to want to go to” 意味着 “difficult to arouse interest”，“limited size” 对应 “smaller”。

句子 (Section D) "‘NASA isn’t going to want to go to something that is smaller than our spaceships,’ says engineer Dan Mazanek..."

Q22

解析 E段中 Nuth 认为用“无人飞船（unmanned spacecraft）”研究小行星要便宜得多，因此把小行星带回地球不够划算（inefficient），对应选项 G。

干扰 他强调“可以更便宜地做（done much more cheaply）”，反衬出捕捉小行星这一方法“不高效（not efficient）”。

句子 (Section E) "Investigations of asteroids can be done much more cheaply with an unmanned spacecraft, says chemist Joseph A. Nuth..."

Q23

句子 (Section B) "An asteroid would provide a stationary base from which to launch missions further into space."

解析 题目说小行星可以充当进一步太空旅行的____，原文 B 段说它提供了一个“stationary base（固定基地）”，填 base。

干扰 “Act as” 对应原文的 “provide”，定位非常直接。

Q24

解析 题目说小行星有较弱的____，允许资源更容易移动，原文 B 段说地球有强“gravity”，而小行星上“far weaker”，填 gravity。

干扰 必须填名词，原文 contrast（对比）了地球的 strong force of gravity 和小行星的 weaker (gravity)。

句子 (Section B) "...because of our planet’s strong force of gravity. Since this would be far weaker on an asteroid..."

Q25

解析 题目说资源包括____，可用于太空或地球，原文 B 段提到“Some are rich in metals, which can be mined... or brought back to Earth”，填 metals。

干扰 题目是复数“resources include...”，且后面有“used on Earth”的定语从句，定位到原文的 metals。

句子 (Section B) "Some are rich in metals, which can be mined and used to build space-based habitats, or brought back to Earth."

Q26

解析 题目说还有____，可被消耗或作为动力来源，原文 B 段提到“Others are up to one-quarter water... used for life-support or... make fuel”，填 water。

干扰 虽然原文出现了“fuel”，但那是“make fuel（制造燃料）”，作为资源的本体是“water”。题目问的是“resources include...”，所以填资源名称。

句子 (Section B) "Others are up to one-quarter water, which could be either be used for life-support or broken down... to make fuel."
